propositions.text: This is an application for leave and judicial review under subsection 72(1) of IRPA of a Refugee Protection Division decision dated April 8, 2014.
propositions.quote: This is an application for leave and judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (the Board) dated April 8, 2014

propositions.text: The application should be allowed for the reasons that follow.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I am of the view that the application should be allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of a 2014 Refugee Protection Division decision and that the application should be allowed.

propositions.text: The applicant was born in Côte d’Ivoire in 1977 and alleges FPI membership since 1998.
propositions.quote: The applicant was born in Côte d’Ivoire in 1977. He alleges that he has been a member of the Front Populaire Ivoirien (FPI) [Ivorian Popular Front] since 1998.

propositions.text: The FPI governed Côte d’Ivoire from 2000 to 2010 and is now the main opposition party after the 2010-2011 crisis.
propositions.quote: The FPI is a political party that governed the country from 2000 to 2010, and which is now the main opposition party since the Ivorian crisis of 2010-2011.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges FPI membership since 1998; the court notes FPI governed 2000-2010 and is now main opposition.

propositions.text: Between 2000-2002 in Bouaké, the applicant held deputy and section secretary positions in the FPI while working as a houseboy.
propositions.quote: The applicant alleges that between 2000 and 2002, when he was living in Bouaké, he held the positions of [translation] “deputy” and [translation] “section secretary” within the FPI. During this period, he worked days as a houseboy.

propositions.text: On September 19, 2002, rebel soldiers tried to kill him at home but he was at a political meeting in Abidjan; rebels ransacked his home.
propositions.quote: On the night of September 19, 2002, the very day of the beginning of the civil war that led to the partition of the country, the applicant claims that rebel soldiers went to his home in order to kill him, but that he was away at a political meeting in Abidjan at the time. The rebels apparently ransacked his place.

propositions.text: He alleges he was targeted for his political activities within the FPI.
propositions.quote: He alleges that he was targeted for his political activities within the FPI.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges holding FPI positions 2000-2002, surviving a rebel attack on his home in 2002 due to political activities.

propositions.text: After these incidents, the applicant moved to Abidjan and was active in FPI youth rallies and organizing meetings 2002-2006.
propositions.quote: Following these incidents, the applicant moved to Abidjan. He participated in FPI youth rallies in 2002, and he was active in the committee that organized meetings and sit-ins of the Jeunesse du Front Populaire Ivoirien [youth wing of the Ivorian Popular Front] between 2003 and 2006.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant moved to Abidjan and was active in FPI youth activities from 2002 to 2006.

propositions.text: On February 14, 2009, rebel soldiers attacked the applicant's vehicle after an FPI gathering; police complaint was ignored.
propositions.quote: On February 14, 2009, the applicant was reportedly attacked by rebel soldiers when he was leaving a gathering of his FPI colleagues at the national television studios, where they had issued a statement in support of ending the partition of the country. The rebel soldiers purportedly shot at his vehicle. That same day, he filed a complaint with the police that was not followed up.

propositions.text: The applicant claims police were in league with his attackers.
propositions.quote: The applicant claims that the police were in league with his attackers.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges a 2009 rebel attack on his vehicle and police complicity in ignoring his complaint.

propositions.text: In 2009, the applicant got a domestic worker job with an Ivorian diplomat in Canada and arrived August 25, 2009.
propositions.quote: In 2009, the applicant received an offer of employment as a domestic worker for an Ivorian diplomat in Canada. Thus, he obtained an entry visa and arrived in Canada on August 25, 2009.

propositions.text: He joined the FPI’s Canadian section after arriving in Canada.
propositions.quote: He subsequently joined the FPI’s Canadian section.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant came to Canada in 2009 as a domestic worker and joined the FPI's Canadian section.

propositions.text: In August 2012, employer returned to Côte d’Ivoire; applicant filed refugee claim September 19, 2012.
propositions.quote: In August 2012, his employer was called back to Côte d’Ivoire. The applicant submitted his refugee protection claim on September 19, 2012.

propositions.text: Applicant refused to return fearing persecution due to FPI membership and political activities in Côte d’Ivoire and Canada.
propositions.quote: The applicant states that he refused to return to Côte d’Ivoire with his employer because he fears for his live if he was to return, particularly in light of the fact that the FPI has since lost power and its activities are violently suppressed by the current regime. He asserts that other FPI members that were close to him have been imprisoned, including his close assistant, and that he fears that the same fate awaits him. He fears persecution by reason of his political opinion and activities based not only on his experiences in Côte d’Ivoire during the decade prior to his departure to work in Canada, but also because of his membership in the FPI in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant filed refugee claim in 2012, fearing persecution due to FPI membership and political activities in Côte d’Ivoire and Canada.

propositions.text: At hearing March 31, 2014, applicant produced documents including FPI Canada membership card; explained lack of Côte d’Ivoire card due to war.
propositions.quote: The hearing was held on March 31, 2014. At that time, the applicant had adduced a number of documents, including a copy of his membership card of the FPI in Canada. The member asked him if he had a membership card for the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire. The applicant explained that he had obtained one in 1998, but that he had left it in Bouaké as he had “to leave hurriedly”. He had not asked for another one in Abidjan because, due to the war, the party had other priorities than issuing membership cards.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker records the applicant's explanation for lacking an FPI membership card from Côte d’Ivoire due to war.

propositions.text: The refugee form stated FPI membership from 2003-2006 and FPI Canada from March 2010; applicant explained omission of earlier membership as leaving Bouaké in 2003.
propositions.quote: The member also raised the issue of the refugee application form he had filled out on October 3, 2012. In answer to the question “Have you ever been a member of an organization?”, he stated that he had been a member of Jeunesse du Front Populaire [Popular Front Youth] from 2003 to 2006, and then of the Front Populaire Ivoirien (FPI-Canada) as of March 2010. When asked why he had failed to indicate that he had been a member of the FPI since 1998 on the form, the applicant explained that he had written down 2003 as a reference date because it was at that time that he left Bouaké and joined the party’s section in Abidjan.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes the applicant's explanation for not listing FPI membership before 2003 on the refugee form.

propositions.text: Applicant explained knowledge of attempted killing on Sept 19, 2002 from colleagues and political context of rebel-controlled Bouaké.
propositions.quote: Regarding the events of September 19, 2002, the member asked the applicant how he knew that people were looking to kill him if he was not there at the time. The applicant explained that he knew other party members who had been in Bouaké at that time, and that two colleagues had contacted him by telephone. He explained that he thought he had been targeted for death because that night [translation] “there were people killed, one was a former president and head of state and the other was a minister of the republic”, and that anyone who did not support Alassane Ouattara, leader of the Rassemblement des républicains de la Côte d’Ivoire (RDR – the party currently in power in Côte d’Ivoire) had fled rebel-controlled areas, of which Bouaké was one. He reiterated that he was targeted by reason of his political activities within the FPI. He explained that his assistant, Némié Taloo, had disappeared that night.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant explained how he knew of the 2002 attack and reiterated political targeting; his assistant disappeared that night.

propositions.text: Applicant reported 3-4 threats from opponents 2003-2006, interpreted as death threats, omitted from personal information form as possible omission.
propositions.quote: With respect to his political activities between 2003 and 2006, the member asked if he had ever encountered any problems. The applicant replied that there had been three or four threats of intimidation of the part of opponents of the party, who said [translation] “You there – well, the day will come when things will go really badly for you.” Asked whether he interpreted this as a death threat, the applicant replied that yes, he did consider this to be a threat against his life. When it was pointed out to him that he had not indicated these threats in his personal information form, the applicant stated that he had failed to indicate this [translation] “perhaps by simple omission”.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant reported threats 2003-2006, considered death threats, but omitted them from forms possibly by omission.

propositions.text: Applicant said rebel forces shot at his vehicle in 2009 after anti-partition statement; he was sure attackers were rebels though unknown personally.
propositions.quote: As to the incidents of February 14, 2009, the applicant reiterated that members of the rebellion had shot at his vehicle just after he had made a statement against the partition on national television. Asked how he knew they were rebel forces rather than [translation] “non-ideological gangsters”, the applicant replied that he was sure they were rebels, given the statement he had just given on the country’s partition, although he did not personally know these attackers.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant said rebels shot at his vehicle in 2009 after his statement; he was sure they were rebels though unknown personally.

propositions.text: Applicant expected police to investigate 2009 attack but thought police were complicit due to no investigations and prior mistreatment.
propositions.quote: With regard to the complaint he had reportedly made to the police about the incident, the member asked several timed what he had expected of the police given that he was unable to identify the gunmen, to which he replied that he expected the police to at least conduct an investigation. He explained that he thought the police officers were in league with his attackers, because on several occasions, the police had [translation] “taken him for a ride” and had not [translation] “carried out any investigations”.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant expected police investigation but thought police complicit due to no investigations and mistreatment.

propositions.text: Luc Gbogouri testified he met applicant in 2009, confirmed applicant's FPI Canada membership and volunteer work, but did not know applicant's prior FPI membership.
propositions.quote: The applicant also had Luc Gbogouri, Secretary-General of the Ottawa-Gatineau section of the FPI, testify. He confirmed that he has known the applicant since 2009, when the latter was looking for organizations of the FPI in Canada, and that the applicant had told him that he had been a member of the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire. Mr. Gbogouri confirmed that the applicant is a member of the FPI in Canada, that he had attended two meetings held by the organization and had worked as a volunteer during the 2010 Ivorian election.

paragraphs.summary: Luc Gbogouri testified he met applicant in 2009, confirmed FPI Canada membership and volunteer work, but not prior FPI membership.

propositions.text: The member found the applicant's narrative about pre-2009 Côte d’Ivoire incidents not credible.
propositions.quote: In his decision, the member dealt principally with the credibility of the applicant’s narrative regarding the incidents that reportedly took place in Côte d’Ivoire before his arrival in Canada in 2009, and concluded that these allegations were not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The member found the applicant's narrative about pre-2009 incidents in Côte d’Ivoire not credible.

propositions.text: The member accepted applicant's FPI Canada membership but found it did not prove FPI Côte d’Ivoire membership.
propositions.quote: In respect to his membership in the FPI in Canada and Luc Gbogouri’s testimony, the member noted that he did not dispute the fact that the applicant had been and remains today a member of the FPI in Canada, but noted that Luc Gbogouri did not know him before he arrived in Canada and that his membership in the FPI in Canada does not establish that he was also a member of the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire.

propositions.text: Applicant registered as FPI Canada member in December 2009, four months after arriving in Canada in August 2009.
propositions.quote: The member noted that the applicant only registered as a member of the FPI in Canada in December 2009, some four months after he arrived in Canada.

propositions.text: The member summarized evidence of applicant's FPI Canada membership and Gbogouri's testimony, which did not confirm prior FPI Côte d’Ivoire membership.
propositions.quote: [26] He registered in Canada as a member of the FPI in December 2009. He participated in meetings of this party in December 2009 and in June 2012. [27] He was apparently also involved in contacting members of the Ivorian diaspora. [28] In Ottawa, he did not participate in any partisan demonstration. [29] To demonstrate his membership in the FPI here in Canada, the claimant submitted Exhibit P‑3, a membership card of the above party (Federation of Canada – Ottawa – Gatineau), as well as the minutes of two meetings he attended in December 2009 and June 2012 (Exhibit P‑3). [30] Furthermore, the claimant had Luc Gbogouri, Secretary‑General of the FPI in Ottawa, testify. The latter confirmed in his testimony that he met the claimant in December 2009 and confirmed his membership at that moment in the FPI in Canada. [31] He never knew him previously and could not say whether he had been a member of the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire as he was relying only on what the claimant had told him. [32] Therefore, this testimony of Mr. Gbogouri does not establish and cannot confirm the claimant’s allegations in any way. [33] The panel does not challenge the fact that the claimant was and is today a member of the FPI in Canada. His membership does not, however, establish that the latter was a member of the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire. [34] Moreover, the panel, noted that the claimant arrived in Canada in August 2009 and that he registered as a member of the FPI in Canada only in December 2009, that is, about four months later.

paragraphs.summary: The member accepted applicant's FPI Canada membership but found it did not prove prior FPI Côte d’Ivoire membership, noting registration delay.

propositions.text: The member rejected the refugee claim because the applicant did not establish a serious possibility of persecution if returned to Côte d’Ivoire.
propositions.quote: The member therefore rejected the refugee protection claim on the ground that the applicant had not established that he would face a serious possibility of persecution if he were to return to his country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The member rejected the refugee claim for failure to establish serious possibility of persecution if returned.

propositions.text: Applicant raises three issues: adequacy of reasons on sur place risk, credibility, and bias.
propositions.quote: The applicant raises three issues: 1. Is the member’s decision unreasonable by reason of inadequacy of reasons regarding the risk the applicant would face simply for being a current member of the FPI in Canada (“refugee sur place”)? 2. Is the member’s decision regarding the applicant’s credibility unreasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The applicant raises issues of adequacy of reasons on sur place risk, credibility, and bias.

propositions.text: Applicant argues the decision erred on all three issues raised.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the decision is in error with regard to the three issues here.

propositions.text: The court agrees with applicant's criticisms on the first issue and will remit the decision for re-determination.
propositions.quote: I agree with his criticisms regarding the first issue, which requires that I remit the decision for re-determination for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues errors on three issues; court agrees on first and will remit decision for re-determination.

propositions.text: Failure to consider relevant grounds of persecution in sur place refugee claim is a question of law reviewed on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: With regard to the issue of adequacy of reasons in a sur place refugee claim, which is the determinative issue in this case, it is established jurisprudence that the failure to consider relevant grounds of persecution is a question of law and is reviewable on a standard of correctness (Nadarasa v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 752 at para 15, [2012] FCJ No 904 [Nadarasa]; Hannoon v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 448 at para 42, [2012] FCJ No 480 [Hannoon]; Mohajery v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 185 at para 26, [2007] FCJ No 252 [Mohajery]; Ghirmatsion v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 519 at para 49, [2013] 1 FCR 261).

paragraphs.summary: The court states failure to consider relevant persecution grounds in sur place claims is a legal question reviewed on correctness standard.

propositions.text: The term 'refugee sur place' means a person facing persecution upon return due to activities outside or inside the country of refuge.
propositions.quote: The term “refugee sur place” refers to a person who, though not necessarily having been a victim of past persecution in their country of origin, would nonetheless face a serious possibility of persecution upon their return.

propositions.text: Mohajery overturned a Board decision for failing to consider sur place risk from conversion to Christianity in Canada.
propositions.quote: in Mohajery, the Court overturned a decision wherein the Board, having found the applicant’s allegations about practising Christianity in Iran and being persecuted not to be credible, failed to consider whether the applicant’s conversion to Christianity while living in Canada would put him at risk if he were to return to Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains 'refugee sur place' and cites Mohajery where failure to consider sur place risk was overturned.

propositions.text: Failure to consider a ground of persecution in a sur place claim is an error of law warranting court intervention.
propositions.quote: Failure to consider a ground of persecution in a sur place claim for refugee protection is an error of law that warrants the Court’s intervention

propositions.text: Cites cases Urur, Manzila, Jiang, Mohajery, Nadarasa supporting this principle.
propositions.quote: (Urur v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1988] FCJ No 20, 91 NR 146; Manzila v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] FCJ No 1264 at para 4, 165 FTR 313; Jiang v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 635 at para 15, [2008] FCJ No 808; Mohajery, at paras 31, 37-38; Nadarasa, at para 26).

paragraphs.summary: The court states failure to consider sur place persecution grounds is legal error, citing multiple cases.

propositions.text: The Board must consider sur place refugee possibility if evidence shows activities in Canada liable to cause negative consequences on return.
propositions.quote: The Board must consider the possibility that a claimant is a sur place refugee even if this ground is not specifically raised, if “it perceptibly emerges from evidence on the record that the activities liable to entail negative consequences in case of a return, took place in Canada”

propositions.text: Mohajery and Hannoon require this analysis even if applicant is not credible, if trustworthy evidence of activities in Canada exists.
propositions.quote: (Mohajery, at para 31; see also Hannoon, at para 47). This analysis must be done even if the Board finds the applicant not to be credible, insofar as trustworthy evidence establishes activities in Canada in support of the sur place refugee claim (Mohajery, at para 32; Hannoon, at para 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Board must consider sur place refugee claims if evidence shows activities in Canada causing risk, even if applicant is not credible.

propositions.text: Respondent concedes sur place refugee issue was raised and submits member adequately considered it per Newfoundland Nurses’ principles.
propositions.quote: the respondent conceded that the issue as to whether the applicant was a refugee sur place was raised based on the facts of this case. However, the respondent submits that the member adequately considered this issue in his decision having regard to all of the evidence in the record and to the principles set out in the decision of the Supreme Court in Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, [2011] 3 SCR 708 [Newfoundland Nurses’].

paragraphs.summary: The respondent concedes sur place issue was raised and argues the member adequately considered it per Newfoundland Nurses’.

propositions.text: The member did not effectively consider the sur place refugee claim for three reasons.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that the member did not, in effect, consider the sur place refugee claim, for three reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member failed to consider the sur place refugee claim for three reasons.

propositions.text: Member only considered applicant’s activities in Canada to support allegations about Côte d’Ivoire events, not sur place claim.
propositions.quote: it appears from the reasons of the decision that the member solely considered evidence of the applicant’s activities in Canada in order to determine whether these supported his allegations regarding events that reportedly occurred in Côte d’Ivoire.

propositions.text: Member found Luc Gbogouri’s testimony unreliable to confirm applicant’s FPI membership in Côte d’Ivoire.
propositions.quote: He [Luc Gbogouri] never knew him previously and could not say whether he had been a member of the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire as he was relying only on what the claimant had told him.

propositions.text: Member concluded Gbogouri’s testimony does not establish claimant’s allegations and does not confirm FPI membership in Côte d’Ivoire.
propositions.quote: Therefore, this testimony of Mr. Gbogouri does not establish and cannot confirm the claimant’s allegations in any way.

propositions.text: Member accepts claimant’s FPI membership in Canada but says it does not establish membership in Côte d’Ivoire.
propositions.quote: The panel does not challenge the fact that the claimant was and is today a member of the FPI in Canada. His membership does not, however, establish that the latter was a member of the FPI in Côte d’Ivoire.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member only considered Canadian activities to support Côte d’Ivoire allegations and rejected Gbogouri’s testimony on FPI membership in Côte d’Ivoire.

propositions.text: Sur place claim analysis must be done even if applicant is not credible on other matters, if evidence of activities in Canada is trustworthy.
propositions.quote: an analysis of a sur place refugee claim must be done even if the member finds that the applicant is not credible on other matters, insofar as the evidence of the activities in Canada is trustworthy

propositions.text: Member found applicant’s political activities in Canada credible but limited analysis to supporting Côte d’Ivoire allegations, which is an error.
propositions.quote: if the member finds the evidence regarding the applicant’s political activities in Canada to be credible – which is the case here, as the member “does not challenge the fact that the claimant was and is today a member of the FPI in Canada” (paragraph 33 of the decision) – he must assess whether these activities gave rise to a well-founded fear of persecution regardless of the allegations with respect to events in Côte d’Ivoire. By limiting his analysis of the activities in Canada to the issue as to whether these supported the allegations about events in Côte d’Ivoire, the member committed an error in principle.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member erred by limiting credible Canadian activities analysis to supporting Côte d’Ivoire allegations only.

propositions.text: Member failed to assess risk from applicant’s FPI membership in Canada despite relevant evidence and testimony about danger on return.
propositions.quote: the member completely failed to assess the risk the applicant could face from simply being a member of the FPI in Canada... The member therefore had a responsibility to assess this evidence and to determine whether the applicant’s involvement with the FPI in Canada would place him at risk should he return to Côte d’Ivoire.

propositions.text: Member noted applicant had not participated in demonstrations but drew no conclusion on risk if returned to Côte d’Ivoire.
propositions.quote: he did note certain facts which may have been relevant to a risk analysis, such as the fact that the applicant had not participated in demonstrations (paragraph 28 of the decision). However, he draws no conclusion as to the possible effect of such activities in the event the applicant was to be returned to Côte d’Ivoire.

propositions.text: Luc Gbogouri testified FPI sympathizers are targeted in Côte d’Ivoire and applicant would be in danger if returned.
propositions.quote: Luc Gbogouri had described the applicant’s activities within the FPI in Canada and testified that FPI sympathizers are targeted in Côte d’Ivoire, that he himself was officially listed because of his political activities with the FPI in Canada and would be arrested if he was to return to Côte d’Ivoire, and that the applicant would also be in danger.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member failed to assess risk from FPI membership in Canada despite testimony about danger on return.

propositions.text: Newfoundland Nurses’ principles do not apply here as the context differs significantly.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that the principles articulated in Newfoundland Nurses’ do not apply here.

propositions.text: Newfoundland Nurses’ requires courts to respect adjudicative bodies’ process and not substitute reasons but may look to record for reasonableness.
propositions.quote: In that case, the Supreme Court considered the adequacy of reasons of a brief decision of a grievance arbitrator and set out the following principles at paragraphs 15 and 16: [15] In assessing whether the decision is reasonable in light of the outcome and the reasons, courts must show “respect for the decision-making process of adjudicative bodies with regard to both the facts and the law” (Dunsmuir, at para. 48). This means that courts should not substitute their own reasons, but they may, if they find it necessary, look to the record for the purpose of assessing the reasonableness of the outcome. [16] Reasons may not include all the arguments, statutory provisions, jurisprudence or other details the reviewing judge would have preferred, but that does not impugn the validity of either the reasons or the result under a reasonableness analysis. A decision-maker is not required to make an explicit finding on each constituent element, however subordinate, leading to its final conclusion (Service Employees’ International Union, Local No. 333 v. Nipawin District Staff Nurses Assn., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 382, at p. 391). In other words, if the reasons allow the reviewing court to understand why the tribunal made its decision and permit it to determine whether the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes, the Dunsmuir criteria are met. [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Newfoundland Nurses’ principles do not apply here due to different context and explains those principles.

propositions.text: Respondent argues member’s hearing questions show consideration of sur place claim and implicit conclusion of insufficient risk.
propositions.quote: the respondent invites me to consider passages from the hearing transcript in which the member questions Luc Gbogouri about his political activities and those of the applicant within the FPI in Canada and the risk they would face in Côte d’Ivoire, and submits that, if one were to consider the case as a whole, the member did in fact consider the sur place refugee claim and implicitly concluded that the risk was an insufficient one on which to base a refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the member considered the sur place claim and implicitly found insufficient risk based on hearing questions.

propositions.text: The context here differs from Newfoundland Nurses’ as this is inquisitorial with no opposing party and major life impact, requiring detailed reasons.
propositions.quote: First, I find the present context to be completely different that the one in Newfoundland Nurses’, where, following an adversarial proceeding, both parties presented well-supported positions on the issue of the calculation of leave in a collective agreement and the arbitrator wrote a brief analysis in favour of one of those positions. In this context, an analysis of the record will allow for an understanding of the basis of the decision. In this case, the applicant adduced his evidence in the context of an inquisitorial proceeding which, in addition, would have a major impact on his life as he faced removal to Côte d’Ivoire in the event his claim was to be refused. Before the Board, there is no opposing party presenting detailed arguments that would support a refusal. The written reasons of the Commission’s decision are therefore essential in order to understand the reasons for the decision which, moreover, was quite detailed in terms of other elements in the record. Thus, it is not a situation in which the decision-maker issued a decision with few details in a context where the parties were already familiar with the substance of the arguments in support of the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case’s inquisitorial context with no opposing party requires detailed reasons unlike Newfoundland Nurses’ context.

propositions.text: Analysis of entire file does not explain why sur place claim was refused; member failed to make findings on risk evidence.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that an analysis of the file as a whole provides no basis for understanding why the sur place refugee claim was refused. The fact that the member had asked questions at the hearing with regard to the risk Luc Gbogouri and the applicant would face in Côte d’Ivoire indicated that the member may have had an interest in the question during the hearing, but it does not make up for the member’s failure to make findings on the value of that evidence or to explain why it would be insufficient.

propositions.text: It is not the court’s role to guess findings or supply reasons missing from tribunal’s decision.
propositions.quote: It is not the role of this Court to assess that evidence itself and attempt to guess which grounds would support a refusal.

propositions.text: Komolafe explains Newfoundland Nurses does not allow court to supply missing reasons or speculate on tribunal’s thinking.
propositions.quote: As my colleague, Justice Rennie explained in Komolafe v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 431 at para 11, [2013] FCJ No 449: [11] Newfoundland Nurses is not an open invitation to the Court to provide reasons that were not given, nor is it licence to guess what findings might have been made or to speculate as to what the tribunal might have been thinking.

propositions.text: Newfoundland Nurses allows courts to connect dots only where lines and direction are clear; here no dots exist.
propositions.quote: Newfoundland Nurses allows reviewing courts to connect the dots on the page where the lines, and the direction they are headed, may be readily drawn. Here, there were no dots on the page.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member’s failure to explain sur place claim refusal cannot be remedied by court guessing, citing Komolafe and Newfoundland Nurses.

propositions.text: Failure to consider sur place refugee claim warrants court intervention.
propositions.quote: I therefore find that the failure to consider the sur place refugee claim warrants the Court’s intervention.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes failure to consider sur place claim warrants intervention.
